text.p: These are the leading stories in the Pakistani press on Wednesday. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
- The cabinet approved a Freedom of Information Ordinance allowing disclosure of records concerning the superior courts and armed forces, areas excluded from the original draft.
- In a crackdown against religious parties, the Punjab provincial police on Tuesday night rounded up 150 activists belonging to militant Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem groups.
- Pager services resumed operations in Karachi after remaining off for about 18 months.

- The U.S. Export-Import (Exim) Bank said it has stopped processing a loan for an oil refinery project in Pakistan, allegedly being set up by friends of Asif Ali Zardari, the spouse of ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto.
- President Farooq Leghari said small groups of religious fanatics in Pakistan, or the Taleban in Afghanistan, could not harm Islamabad's cordial ties with Iran.
- Pakistan will buy bulldozers from Iran in exchange for a sugar plant.
- Pakistan may hold the private sector meeting of the Islamic Chamber of Commrce and Industry this year.
- Pakistan's gold and silver importer, ARY Traders, which had suspended gold imports, has decided to resume supply early next week.
- Funds for the state-run Chashma Nuclear Power Plant and the People's Steel Mills have been fully restored, despite World Bank objections.

- The State (central) Bank of Pakistan's Governor Mohammad Yaqub expressed confidence that the three ordinances issued by President Farooq Leghari on Tuesday would ensure complete autonomy to the bank as the final monetary authority of the country, with powers to control the banking system and set limits on credit supply to federal and provincial governments.
- The European Union has raised duty on seafood exports from Pakistan to 5.2 percent from 4.5 percent.

- The caretaker government, which had cancelled a multi-million dollar contract for the computerisation of national identity card with the International Business Machines (IBM), has restored it under pressure from the United States.
